column2: “Your objection is reasonable, Miss Luo. But if you knew where the furniture was intended to go, you would not object. There are all sorts of palaces, far more than the familiar Three Palaces and Six Courts. The furnishings differ greatly according to the place and its purpose. If everything had the same dragons and phoenixes, people would grow tired of looking at them. Wouldn't you agree?” “There is something in that. Where was this set to be used, then?” “At the Yuanmingyuan…” “Mr Li, you really do take me for a country bumpkin! Who doesn't know that the foreign devils burned the Yuanmingyuan down?” “What has been burned can be rebuilt. Of course, if it really had been rebuilt, this furniture would not be here.”

According to Mr Li, some men from the Imperial Household Department and the eunuchs in charge of palace affairs had argued that, since the uprising of Hong and Yang had been defeated and the Nian armies crushed, there was no longer any cause for concern. They had therefore urged Empress Dowager Cixi: “In another three or four years, the emperor will come of age. Once the two great ceremonies of his marriage and assumption of personal rule are over, the two empress dowagers ought to have somewhere to spend their later years in comfort. The Yiheyuan could perfectly well be restored. Her Majesty is supported by the whole empire. Building a garden is hardly excessive.” Cixi was tempted, and the young emperor, then twelve or thirteen, was even more enthusiastic. When word spread, a prefect who had come from the Imperial Household Department and served several lucrative terms in Guangdong was quick to seize the opportunity. He commissioned a special set of suanzhi furniture with mother-of-pearl inlay as tribute. While it was being shipped north by sea, however, circumstances changed. The scheme had been discussed privately for several months. Prince Gong, who was directing the government, strongly disapproved but could not say so openly. At the two empress dowagers' regular daily audiences, he therefore kept stressing that the great disorders had only just been suppressed, countless neglected affairs needed attention, and the treasury was in difficulty. He hoped Cixi would abandon the idea herself. While he was pursuing this patient campaign, news arrived of a prefect sending furniture as tribute for use at the Yiheyuan. Furious, he instructed a Manchu censor to impeach the man with a detailed account of proven corruption. Prince Gong personally asked for his dismissal and investigation. Cixi could hardly protect him and granted the request. The prefect was imprisoned. Naturally, there was no longer any reason to ship the tribute north. His younger brother, who was escorting it, unloaded it in Shanghai and sold it. That was how it had come to Changfa.

“There were three sets in all: one for a reception hall, one for a study, and this one. The first two have been sold. An expectant circuit intendant from Jiangxi came to see this set the day before yesterday. He loved it, but hadn't brought enough money and asked me to keep it for ten days. Since he paid no deposit, I need not consider him. If you like it, Miss Luo, I shall give you an especially modest price. To tell you the truth, very few people can afford to use furniture like this. If a bedroom is furnished so splendidly, what must the main hall, garden drawing room and study contain? That is why this set is so difficult to sell.” Luo thought that, by his account, perhaps only Hu's household could use it. She had not imagined that an expectant circuit intendant from Jiangxi might be equally wealthy. Then it occurred to her that Hu himself held that designation. Could he have sent someone to look at it? “What is this gentleman's surname? He must be able to afford it.” “Zhu. But Circuit Intendant Zhu was not buying it for himself. He meant to present it to a governor-general's mother.” An idea stirred in Luo's mind. “What is your price?” “Fifteen hundred taels, at cost. In fact, even selling at cost means losing the interest on the money tied up in it. Still, I have made my profit on the other two sets. I don't mind losing a little on this one.”

“I will offer you a round thousand, Mr Li.” He smiled wryly. “Miss Luo, you are taking away a third of the price. That is ruthless bargaining.” “The seller asks for the sky; the buyer offers the ground. Plenty of bargains are made by halving the price and then halving it again.” “From your accent, are you from Hangzhou?” “Yes. Why do you ask?” “You Hangzhou people bargain hard. Halving it twice means taking away three quarters. Where in the world can anyone do business like that? You must raise your offer a little, Miss Luo.” After several increases, they settled on twelve hundred taels. Luo had brought banknotes. Taking out one for four hundred taels and holding it in her hand, she laid down a condition. “This sale can go through only if you do as I say. Tomorrow I shall bring someone to look. If you are asked the price, say eight hundred taels.” “Why?” “Never mind that. You want twelve hundred. I shall pay you four hundred today and another eight hundred tomorrow, not a cash less. But you must state clearly on the receipt that you will follow my instructions. If you don't, the sale is cancelled and you must return double the deposit.” “Certainly. I shall do as you say.” Mr Li accepted the deposit and wrote the receipt. Shortly after Luo left, another regular customer arrived.

“Mrs Gu! Here is my God of Wealth again. What would you like to see today?” “Let me look around first.” Mr Li showed her from one area to another. When they reached the suanzhi set with mother-of-pearl inlay, she stopped. “How much is this?” “I am sorry, Mrs Gu. It has just been sold…” Deeply disappointed but unwilling to give up, the Seventh Lady asked, “To whom? What an unlucky coincidence!” Mr Li considered the situation. He had intended to add, “Miss Luo has just bought it,” but Mrs Gu had cut him short. She looked determined to have it. If he named Luo, she would certainly ask her to yield it, and that would make things awkward. Miss Luo was formidable; the less he provoked her, the better. Having reached this conclusion, he said nothing. But the more the Seventh Lady looked, the more she liked the furniture and the less willing she was to let it go. “What price did you sell it for?” “Since it has been sold, there is no need to ask, Mrs Gu.” Her face hardened, and she began to give him a dressing-down on the spot. “What is wrong with asking? Has your business grown so large that you have become too grand for us, Mr Li? Or are you growing more muddle-headed with age? Who ever heard of doing business like this, when a customer may not even ask a question?” “Please don't scold me.” An inspiration came to him. His rueful smile vanished, and he asked calmly, “May I first ask you a couple of questions?”

“Of course. Why not?” “Do you want this furniture for yourself or as a gift?” “A gift.” “For whom?” “Never mind.” “If you tell me, perhaps something can be arranged.” “Very well. For the Miss Luo who came here with me last time.” Now Mr Li understood. This was the person Luo intended to bring. Smiling, he said, “What a coincidence indeed! The customer who has just bought it was Miss Luo herself.” The Seventh Lady was astonished. So Luo had been here? “She bought this set?” she asked quickly. “For how much?” “Eight hundred taels.” She nodded. “A fair enough price. How much deposit did she leave?” “None.” “None?” Her temper rose again. “Then why wouldn't you sell it to me?” “In business, a promise must count. Miss Luo came through you, Mrs Gu. Naturally, I trust her.” The Seventh Lady liked the sound of that and told him the truth. “Mr Li, Miss Luo is going to be a bride. I am buying the furniture for her dowry. She probably didn't want me to spend the money, so she came to choose it herself. Tomorrow I shall bring her here. Don't accept her money. Take mine.”

“Certainly.” “One more thing. You promised her eight hundred taels, and eight hundred it must remain. But I shall bargain with you. It will only be pretence. I shall pay you two hundred today. Tomorrow, when I bargain you down to six hundred, say that you cannot refuse an old customer and agree. I don't want her to feel bad about my spending so much. Do you understand?” “Of course! Miss Luo must have earned the blessing of a friend like you in a previous life. You buy her dowry furniture and still take care to spare her feelings. No one could be more generous and considerate, Mrs Gu.” The Seventh Lady was already pleased with herself for securing such fine furniture. His praise made her happier still. She paid the deposit and went home in high spirits, telling Gu Yingchun how satisfactorily everything had worked out. When Luo arrived the next day, her first words were, “You went to Changfa yesterday?” Luo had no idea how she had found out, but answered composedly, “Yes.” “You chose a set of furniture and settled the price?” “Yes. Eight hundred taels.” “Then nothing could be better. You have a very good eye. Let us go.”

They drove to Changfa together. Mr Li had tea, tobacco, fruit and refreshments ready. After sitting for a little while, they went to inspect the furniture. “Miss Luo says she has settled the price with you. Is that right?” “Yes.” “That was when Miss Luo was buying. Now I am the buyer. We have dealt with each other for years, Mr Li. You ought to make a special concession. I offer six hundred taels.” “Mrs Gu, I am already losing money.” “I know. I am forcing another two hundred off the price only because we have been dealing with each other for so long.” “Next time I shall certainly show consideration. This time, however, my quoted price must stand. It cannot be changed.” His refusal was absolute. The Seventh Lady turned pale with fury. She wanted to give him a thorough tongue-lashing, but this was a wedding purchase, no occasion for a quarrel; besides, she could not bear to lose such fine furniture. Swallowing her anger, she laughed bitterly. “Very well. You win.” She took out banknotes for eight hundred taels and flung them onto the table. “Please don't be angry, Mrs Gu. I have a real difficulty. I shall come to your house another day to explain and apologize.” “Who wants your apology? Let me tell you, this is the last chance you will have to fleece me.” She turned and left. Mr Li hurried after her to explain, but she ignored him. She and Luo drove home, the Seventh Lady so angry that she scarcely spoke. Luo found the whole affair deeply unpleasant too.

At home they found Gu in the sitting room. Seeing his wife's unhappy expression, he smiled and asked, “You went out so cheerfully. Why do you look so displeased now?” “Mr Li of Changfa doesn't know how to behave!” she declared loudly. “Never give him any more business. You said you would take a foreigner there to order furniture. Don't bother. Choose another shop.” “What did he do?” “He…” She paused. “He insisted on eight hundred taels.” “Did you pay?” “What do you think?” She had told Gu about paying the difference in advance. He knew that Mr Li had a large business and, though shrewd, was reliable. It seemed unlikely that he would simply pocket an extra two hundred taels. Perhaps there was another explanation. With Luo present, however, Gu could not pursue the matter and remained silent.

Luo tried to soothe her friend. “The furniture really is good, Seventh Sister. Eight hundred taels is very reasonable. Calm down first. I want to discuss a use I have in mind for it.” Before the Seventh Lady could reply, the maid came in to announce that Mr Li had arrived and wished to see her. “I won't see him.” “I will,” Gu said. “Let me question him.” He returned shortly afterwards, smiling broadly and carrying a red envelope. The Seventh Lady took it. On the label were the words “Wedding Gift,” with Mr Li's name below. Inside was a banknote for two hundred and forty taels. “What is this supposed to mean?” “It is not for you,” Gu said. “You told me Miss Luo was to be a bride, didn't you? This is his wedding present.” Taken completely by surprise, the two women exchanged bewildered looks, then urged him with their eyes to go on. But Gu seemed barely able to contain his laughter. His wife gave him a sharp look. “What are you laughing at? Tell us!” “How could I not laugh? Only people who think as deeply as you two could manage something like this.”

Gu glanced at Luo, then told his wife, “Do you know what the furniture costs? Twelve hundred taels.” “Oh!” Luo exclaimed. “Brother-in-Law Gu, he told you?” “Of course. How else could he explain taking a further two hundred as deposit and then flatly refusing to acknowledge it?” “You had already paid him two hundred, Seventh Sister?” The Seventh Lady stared for a moment, then understood. “And you had paid four hundred first?” “Yes.” “Why?” “I didn't want you to spend too much.” The Seventh Lady burst out laughing. “We both took the same road! I knew you didn't want me to spend too much, so I paid him two hundred beforehand. I was wondering how such fine things could be so cheap.” Luo found it amusing too. “Brother-in-Law Gu is right. Only people who think too hard would do this. I kept it from you; you kept it from me; we both reasoned ourselves into a corner. Still, Mr Li was not quite right either. Why didn't he simply take two hundred less at the time, instead of making you angry for nothing?” “He has an explanation,” Gu replied. “Let me repeat his words. He said, ‘That Miss Luo looks a very formidable woman. I had to be on my guard. The receipt expressly says I must quote eight hundred taels, and if I change my words I must return double the deposit. Suppose I altered the price, and she produced the receipt and struck me with it like the Heaven-Overturning Seal? I would have no defence. That is why I would not give way. I preferred to offend Mrs Gu and come afterwards to apologize.’”

The Seventh Lady's resentment vanished. “He does know how to behave, after all,” she said happily. “He has even added forty taels as a wedding gift.” She handed the red envelope to Luo. “I don't want it. It isn't mine.” Luo refused to take it. “Then is it mine? I am not the one becoming a bride!” the Seventh Lady joked. Luo smiled in embarrassment but still refused, leaving her friend's hand suspended between them. “Give it to me,” Gu said. “Two hundred is the returned deposit, and forty is the wedding gift. I shall have them entered in the accounts.” His wife handed him the envelope, then began praising the suanzhi furniture with its mother-of-pearl inlay. Even twelve hundred taels, she thought, was not too much for it.

They went on to discuss the furniture's history. Its value could no longer be measured simply in silver. Luo had therefore formed a plan. Even if it were part of her dowry, such a set seemed too grand for her own use and might attract criticism. She privately proposed to the Seventh Lady that she present it to Old Madam Hu. “It was something Mr Li said that gave me the idea. A Circuit Intendant Zhu from Jiangxi had wanted to buy it for a governor-general's mother. I thought: if I use it and Old Madam Hu's furniture is not as fine, I shall feel uncomfortable. Better to offer borrowed flowers to the Buddha and turn it into a gift. You won't blame me, will you, Seventh Sister?” “Of course not.” The Seventh Lady was deeply pleased. “To tell the truth, seeing how well you understand people sets my mind at rest. There are so many people and so much gossip in the Hu household. I was afraid you might feel that, since you had done nothing wrong, you could be too outspoken and offend them.” “One cannot avoid offending people. As long as certain people are not offended, that is enough. Old Madam Hu, for instance, must be very well attended to.” The Seventh Lady nodded inwardly. Luo must understand the principle of holding the emperor in one's power to command the feudal lords, she thought. Luo knew not only how to deal with people but how to practise the art of government. Worrying about her had been quite unnecessary.
